blocks.code:
==19182== Invalid write of size 4
==19182==    at 0x804838F: f (example.c:6)
==19182==    by 0x80483AB: main (example.c:11)
==19182==  Address 0x1BA45050 is 0 bytes after a block of size 40 alloc'd
==19182==    at 0x1B8FF5CD: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:130)
==19182==    by 0x8048385: f (example.c:5)
==19182==    by 0x80483AB: main (example.c:11)

==19182== 40 bytes in 1 blocks are definitely lost in loss record 1 of 1
==19182==    at 0x1B8FF5CD: malloc (vg_replace_malloc.c:130)
==19182==    by 0x8048385: f (a.c:5)
==19182==    by 0x80483AB: main (a.c:11)
blocks.caption: From the Valgrind Quick Start Guide (not run here). The program mallocs 10 ints, writes x[10] and never frees x. 19182 is the process ID.

blocks.md:
How to read it: the first line names the error (an *invalid write* of 4 bytes, one int); the `at`/`by` lines are a backtrace, innermost first; the `Address ... is 0 bytes after a block of size 40` part says the write landed just past the end of a 40-byte block, and where that block was allocated. That is the same information ASan gave you in lesson 11, in a different layout.

The leak report says where the leaked block was allocated, not why it leaked. *Definitely lost* means no pointer to the block remains anywhere: fix it. The guide also suggests fixing errors in the order they are reported, since later errors can be caused by earlier ones.

blocks.title: Which tool for which C bug

scenes.caption: A crash, a wrong answer or a suspected leak. Start with the cheapest tool and move down.
Warnings cost nothing and catch whole classes of bugs before the program runs: format mismatches, sign comparisons, returning a local's address.
Memory errors and UB on the paths you run: rebuild with sanitizers. Clang's docs give ASan's typical slowdown as 2x. On Linux, ASan also reports leaks at exit.

Valgrind memcheck runs the existing binary on a synthetic CPU, so no rebuild is needed (use -g for line numbers), at about 20 to 30 times slower. It runs on Linux and some other systems, not on Apple Silicon Macs.
Logic bugs and crashes you need to understand: a debugger. Stop at the crash or a breakpoint, read the backtrace and the variables, step forward, and watch values change.

blocks.md: On the Mac used for this course, the ASan runtime in Apple's clang refused leak detection: running with `ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1` printed `detect_leaks is not supported on this platform`. On Linux, ASan's leak check is on by default. Check leaks where your tools support them, for example in Linux CI.

Build with `-g -O0` when debugging. Read a backtrace from frame #0 down to your own code, then use breakpoints, next, step, finish and print to see why the state went wrong. Use watchpoints for 'who changed this', and Valgrind when you cannot rebuild.

blocks.question: A crash report shows `#0 nth crash.c:18` and `#1 main crash.c:27`. Which statement is right?
options: main crashed, and nth was the last function it called
The bug must be on line 18, because frame #0 is always the culprit
Line 27 ran after line 18
The crash happened in nth at line 18, called from main at line 27; the cause may be in either
blocks.explain: Frame #0 is where execution stopped and #1 is its caller. The faulting line is where the bad pointer was used, not necessarily where the mistake was made: here main passed an index that was out of range.

blocks.question: A third-party library, shipped only as a compiled binary, seems to corrupt the heap in your Linux service. You cannot recompile it. Which tool fits first?
options: AddressSanitizer, by adding -fsanitize=address to your own build
Valgrind memcheck on the existing binary
-Wall -Wextra on your own code
gdb with a breakpoint on main
blocks.explain: Valgrind instruments the program at run time, including code in libraries you did not compile, so no rebuild is needed. ASan only instruments code compiled with the flag, and warnings only see your source. A debugger helps once you know where to look.
